claims.text: Conventional W–Cu composites consist of consolidated tungsten and copper phases with unmodified native interfaces.
The proposed intervention is to apply a few-nanometer-thick graphene coating to tungsten particles before composite consolidation.
A few-nanometer-thick carbide coating is proposed as an alternative to graphene.
High thermal loads, cyclic heating, and neutron irradiation are representative conditions for heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
A uniform ultrathin coating will improve bonding at the tungsten–copper interface.
The coating will enhance phonon coupling across the tungsten–copper interface.
The coating will enhance electron coupling across the tungsten–copper interface.
The conformal coating will reduce tungsten–copper interfacial thermal resistance by providing improved lattice and electronic continuity.
Keeping the bulk tungsten and copper phases intact will preserve mechanical toughness.
Keeping the bulk tungsten and copper phases intact will preserve irradiation resilience.
A graphene-coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
A carbide-coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The modified W–Cu composite will retain mechanical strength on par with the uncoated baseline.
The modified W–Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance on par with the uncoated baseline.
Unmodified W–Cu composites have relatively high thermal resistance at tungsten–copper boundaries.
The predicted benefit requires a uniform nanometer-scale coating that does not alter the volume fraction or connectivity of the bulk phases.
Excessive coating thickness or coating inhomogeneity could compromise mechanical or irradiation properties.
